A_target.statement:
Let $G$ be a [[Definition:Locally Compact Space|locally compact]] [[Definition:Abelian Group|abelian]] [[Definition:Topological Group|topological group]] with [[Definition:Pontryagin Dual|dual]] $\hat G$.
Then the evaluation map:
:$\alpha: G \to \hat {\hat G}, \quad \map {\map \alpha g} \chi = \map \chi g$
is an [[Definition:Isomorphism of Topological Groups|isomorphism of topological groups]].

B_source.statement:
Let $G$ be a [[Definition:Topological Group|topological group]].
The [[Definition:Character (Group Theory)|characters]] of $G$, the continuous homomorphisms $G \to \Bbb T$, form a group under pointwise multiplication.

substitutions.a homomorphism between groups: the induced homomorphism between duals, in the reverse direction
substitutions.evaluating a character at an element: evaluating an element at a character, after the roles are exchanged

derived.the natural map into the double dual: sending an element to evaluation at it
derived.the double dual being isomorphic to the: the evaluation map is an isomorphism of topological groups

validity_conditions: The dual carries a topology of uniform convergence on compact sets, under which it is again locally compact abelian, so the construction can be iterated.
The evaluation map into the double dual is defined without any choices, which is what makes the isomorphism natural rather than merely an isomorphism of abstract groups.
Local compactness is essential: for general topological abelian groups the characters may fail to separate points and the evaluation map need not be injective.
proof_plan: Form $\hat G$, the group of continuous homomorphisms $G \to \Bbb T$, with the [[Definition:Compact-Open Topology|topology of uniform convergence on compact sets]].
$\hat G$ is again locally compact abelian, so the construction iterates to give $\hat {\hat G}$.

Define $\map {\map \alpha g} \chi = \map \chi g$.
$\map \alpha g$ is a continuous character of $\hat G$, and $\alpha$ is a continuous homomorphism.

[[Definition:Injection|Injectivity]] follows from the existence of enough characters to separate points, by the [[Gelfand-Raikov Theorem]].
Surjectivity and openness follow from the [[Fourier Inversion Theorem|Fourier inversion]] and [[Plancherel Theorem|Plancherel]] theorems on $G$.
This is [[Pontryagin Duality Theorem|Pontryagin duality]].
{{qed}}
